title: 11/11/2026 | Becky Wied | PC | Project 59142 - Opposition to Synergen's Request for Good Cause Exception Relating to Batch Zero Eligibility Deadlines

documents.text:
=== Opposition to Synergen's Request for Good Cause Exception To Batch Zero Eligibility Deadline.pdf ===
                          Before the Public Utility Commission of Texas

              PUCT Project No. 59142 - ERCOT Batch Zero Eligibility Deadlines

                 Review of ERCOT's Interconnection Processes for Large Loads

   Public Comments Opposing Synergen Green Energy, Inc.'s Request for Good Cause
               Exception Relating to Batch Zero Eligibility Deadlines

I submit these comments in opposition to Synergen Green Energy, Inc.'s request for a good cause
exception allowing its proposed Calhoun County green ammonia facility to be included in
ERCOT's Batch Zero process despite missing the established eligibility deadlines.

Synergen’s explanation for missing the deadlines is that it was generally unaware of the new
requirements, had no prior experience with ERCOT's interconnection process, and relied on the
local electric cooperative to guide it.

I do not believe those explanations are sufficient.

A company proposing a large load interconnection agreement has a responsibility to understand
and monitor the regulatory requirements that govern its development. An applicant describing a
project involving hundreds of millions in investment and approximately 300 MW of electric
demand is not a small undertaking, and the company should be expected to have the professional
and regulatory resources necessary to track applicable rules and deadlines.

Being unaware of and not able to qualify under the new rules should not be an acceptable excuse
for a company undertaking a project of this size.

An applicant’s prior expenditure should not support an exception to the financial security
requirement. Money already spent on project development is not the same as satisfying a
financial security requirement established for large-load applicants. Prior expenditures should
not automatically excuse compliance or give one applicant an advantage over others.

A company also asking to delay posting the required financial security until its load study is
completed and it reaches Final Investment Decision, is in effect, wanting to proceed through the
Batch Zero process before meeting a requirement intended to evaluate the readiness and financial
commitment of large-load projects.

I recognize that the new deadlines were implemented on a compressed schedule. That
circumstance deserves consideration. However, it does not eliminate a developer's responsibility
to stay informed, particularly when it has been pursuing a major electric interconnection.

The Commission should also consider the precedent this would establish. If companies can miss
established deadlines and obtain exceptions based on lack of awareness, reliance on another
party, or money already spent, the purpose and consistent application of those requirements are
weakened.
 I respectfully ask the Commission to:

   1. Deny any requested good cause exception based on an applicant's asserted lack of
      awareness and lack of prior experience.
   2. Require documentation supporting any claimed investment and assertions regarding
      project readiness and financing.
   3. Apply the same eligibility and financial security requirements to all large applicants.
   4. Avoid granting preferential treatment that undermines consistent enforcement of
      ERCOT's interconnection requirements.

An applicant's investment claims and the potential economic benefits of a proposed project do
not relieve it of its responsibility to comply with applicable regulations and deadlines.

The financial consequences of a missed deadline do not, by themselves, establish good cause for
an exception.

I respectfully request that the Commission deny any such requested relief.

Becky Wied
